interview_metadata.name: Fredick Burley
interview_metadata.protocol: American Voices Project (Park et al. 2024, Table 7) — Full 109 questions

transcript.question_text: To start, I would like to begin with a big question: tell me the story of your life. Start from the beginning -- from your childhood, to education, to family and relationships, and to any major life events you may have had.
transcript.response: I was born and raised in Brooklyn, in Bed-Stuy, back when the neighborhood had a lot of rough edges but also a lot of pride. My parents came up from the South during the Great Migration. My father was from South Carolina and my mother from Georgia, and they carried that Southern discipline with them, along with church manners, Sunday food, and a belief that you did not waste anything. I grew up around Black families, Caribbean families, storefront churches, barber shops, record stores, block associations, all of that. By the time I was a teenager, you could feel the city changing, music changing, politics changing, and young people trying to figure out where they fit. I was not the loudest kid. I was the one taking things apart, keeping score, watching how people moved. I went to public school in Brooklyn, then did an associate's degree in business administration. I did not come from a family where college was automatic, so that degree meant something. I started in retail and service work young, first doing stock, register, back room, then scheduling, inventory, purchasing, and eventually management. I spent over thirty years in operations for a mid-size Brooklyn retail and service business. I never married and I do not have children. There were relationships, some serious enough where marriage was discussed, but I always had a strong pull toward my own space and routine. Over time I became the person younger staff came to when the schedule was a mess or the numbers did not add up. Now I am easing toward consulting, helping smaller businesses make sense of inventory, staffing, and budgets without making things too complicated. Outside of work, I keep a quieter life: jazz records, photography, woodworking, balcony herbs, reading history, and trying to understand where my family came from.

follow_ups.question: When you think of childhood in Bed-Stuy, what scene comes back most clearly?
follow_ups.response: Summer evenings on the stoop. You had older folks watching the block, kids running, somebody playing Marvin Gaye or James Brown from an open window, and my mother calling me in before it got too late.

follow_ups.question: Who shaped you most when you were young?
follow_ups.response: My father shaped my work habits, but my mother shaped my patience. He was about showing up on time; she was about listening before you spoke.

transcript.question_text: Some people tell us that they've reached a crossroads at some points in their life where multiple paths were available, and their choice then made a significant difference in defining who they are. What about you? Was there a moment like that for you, and if so, could you tell me the whole story about that from start to finish?
transcript.response: Yes. The biggest one was in my late twenties. I had a chance to move into a more corporate retail track, out of Brooklyn, with better pay and a more polished title. At the same time, the owner of the local business where I was working asked me to stay and take on operations. It was less glamorous, but I knew the staff, knew the customers, and knew that place could run better if somebody paid attention. I remember sitting at my kitchen table with two yellow pads, writing the pros and cons. The corporate job had money and a ladder. The Brooklyn job had trust, responsibility, and room to learn by doing. I stayed. That choice made me practical. I learned inventory by counting boxes at 6 a.m., learned budgeting by seeing when cash was tight, and learned people by trying to make schedules that did not break them.

follow_ups.question: Did anyone advise you one way or the other?
follow_ups.response: My father said take the stable money. My mother said, 'Which one lets you sleep at night?' That stuck with me.

follow_ups.question: Do you regret not taking the corporate path?
follow_ups.response: Sometimes when I look at retirement savings, yes, a little. But I do not regret the kind of skill and judgment I built.

transcript.question_text: Some people tell us they made a conscious choice or decision in moments like these, while others say it 'just happened'. What about you?
transcript.response: It was conscious. I worried it half to death, made notes, talked to my parents, and then decided I wanted useful responsibility more than a shiny title.

follow_ups.question: How long did you take to decide?
follow_ups.response: About two weeks, though it felt longer because I kept turning it over in my head.

follow_ups.question: What finally settled it?
follow_ups.response: The owner let me redesign the stockroom and schedule system before I even had the title. That told me I would have real authority.

transcript.question_text: Do you think another person or an organization could have lent a helping hand during moments like this?
transcript.response: A mentor outside the business would have helped. I had common sense, but not much guidance about negotiating salary, benefits, or long-term retirement planning.

follow_ups.question: What kind of help would have mattered most?
follow_ups.response: Someone explaining the money side plainly: pension, 401(k), health coverage, and how to ask for more without feeling greedy.

follow_ups.question: Did you later provide that kind of help to others?
follow_ups.response: Yes, especially younger managers. I tell them to get promises written down.

transcript.question_text: Moving to present time, tell me more about family who are important to you. Do you have a partner, or children?
transcript.response: I never married and I do not have children. My parents have both passed, and that changed the shape of my family life. I have a younger sister, Denise, who lives in Queens, and we speak most Sundays. She has two grown children, so I am Uncle Fred to them, though they are adults now with their own schedules. I also have cousins in Brooklyn, New Jersey, and down South. We are not in each other's pockets, but there is a family thread. Thanksgiving or a summer cookout will bring people together. I am the one who remembers dates and family stories, partly because of the genealogy work I do. I have never been the person hosting big gatherings every month, but I show up, bring something practical, and listen. In my day-to-day life, family is more phone calls, text messages, occasional visits, and checking on people than constant togetherness.

follow_ups.question: Who do you rely on most in your family?
follow_ups.response: My sister Denise. She is more social than I am, so she keeps me connected.

follow_ups.question: What do you usually bring to family gatherings?
follow_ups.response: Macaroni and cheese if I have time, or a good bakery pound cake if I am rushing.

transcript.question_text: Are there anyone else in your immediate family whom you have not mentioned? Who are they, and what is your relationship with them like?
transcript.response: Besides Denise, her son Marcus and daughter Tasha are the closest immediate family. We get along well, but I see them more around birthdays and holidays than weekly.

follow_ups.question: Do they come to you for advice?
follow_ups.response: Marcus does sometimes about work. Tasha asks more about family history.

follow_ups.question: Do you visit Queens often?
follow_ups.response: Maybe once every month or two, usually on a Sunday afternoon.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about anyone else in your life we haven't discussed (like friends or romantic partners). Are there people outside of your family who are important to you?
transcript.response: I have a small circle. There is Calvin, an old coworker who meets me for coffee every other Friday. There is Mr. Alvarez from the walking club, and a woman named Ruth from my photography class who will tell me when a local exhibit is worth seeing. I dated someone named Elaine for several years in my forties, and we are friendly but not close now. I am comfortable alone, so friendships with me tend to be steady but not daily.

follow_ups.question: Where do you and Calvin usually meet?
follow_ups.response: A diner on 18th Avenue, early, before it gets crowded.

follow_ups.question: How often do you see Ruth?
follow_ups.response: Maybe once a month, usually at a gallery opening or photo walk.

transcript.question_text: Now let's talk about your current neighborhood. Tell me all about the neighborhood and area in which you are living now.
transcript.response: I live in Brooklyn, in the 11204 area, so Bensonhurst and nearby neighborhoods are part of my daily map. It is a mix of older Italian families, Chinese families, Jewish families, newer renters, delivery workers, retirees, and small businesses. I like that I can walk to groceries, the pharmacy, the train, and a decent bakery. It is not Bed-Stuy, where I grew up, but Brooklyn is still Brooklyn: people know how to make a life in tight spaces. My block is mostly apartment buildings and two-family houses. From my balcony I can hear traffic, kids after school, and sometimes somebody practicing piano badly through an open window.

follow_ups.question: What places do you use most in the neighborhood?
follow_ups.response: The fruit stand, the pharmacy, the hardware store, the library branch, and a small noodle shop when I do not feel like cooking.

follow_ups.question: Do you know your neighbors?
follow_ups.response: A few by name, more by face. I am polite, but I keep boundaries.

transcript.question_text: Some people say they feel really safe in their neighborhoods, others not so much. How about for you?
transcript.response: I feel mostly safe. I pay attention late at night, but I am not afraid walking to the train or coming back from the store.

follow_ups.question: Are there times you avoid going out?
follow_ups.response: Very late, after midnight, unless I really have to.

follow_ups.question: What makes it feel safe?
follow_ups.response: People are around, businesses stay open, and the block has older residents who notice things.

transcript.question_text: Living any place has its ups and downs. Tell me about what it's been like for you living here.
transcript.response: The good part is convenience and variety. The hard part is noise, rent pressure, and the feeling that every familiar little shop can disappear overnight.

follow_ups.question: What change bothers you most?
follow_ups.response: Small stores closing because the rent jumps. You lose more than a store; you lose relationships.

follow_ups.question: What keeps you there?
follow_ups.response: Transit, routine, and the fact that I can live quietly without needing a car.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about the people who live with you right now, even people who are staying here temporarily.
transcript.response: I live alone. It is a one-bedroom with a small spare room I use for woodworking and office things. Nobody is staying with me now. I like having my own kitchen, my own quiet, and my own piles of notes, even if those piles get out of hand.

follow_ups.question: How long have you lived alone?
follow_ups.response: Most of my adult life, aside from a few stretches when I lived with a partner.

follow_ups.question: What is your favorite room?
follow_ups.response: The spare room, because it has my tools, files, photo supplies, and a small desk.

transcript.question_text: Is anyone in your household a temporary member, or is everyone a permanent member of the household?
transcript.response: No temporary members. It is just me.

follow_ups.question: Any planned visitors staying soon?
follow_ups.response: No, just short visits.

follow_ups.question: Do relatives have keys?
follow_ups.response: My sister has a spare key for emergencies.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about anyone else who stays here from time to time, if there is anyone like that
transcript.response: No one stays over regularly.

follow_ups.question: Do family members ever spend the night?
follow_ups.response: Almost never. The apartment is not really set up for guests.

follow_ups.question: Do friends visit?
follow_ups.response: For coffee or to look at photos, not overnight.

transcript.question_text: Is there anyone who usually lives here but is away -- traveling, at school, or in a hospital?
transcript.response: No, nobody else usually lives here.

follow_ups.question: So no one away temporarily?
follow_ups.response: Correct.

follow_ups.question: Any pets?
follow_ups.response: No pets.

transcript.question_text: Right now, across a typical week, how do your days vary?
transcript.response: My weekdays start around 6:30. I make coffee, check the news, water the balcony herbs if the weather calls for it, and look over my notes. I still do part-time consulting and some operations work, usually Tuesday through Thursday. Mondays I use for paperwork, invoicing, errands, and reading. Fridays are lighter, sometimes coffee with Calvin. Saturday morning is pickleball if my knee feels decent, then groceries. Sunday is quieter: laundry, cooking, phone call with my sister, and jazz in the evening.

follow_ups.question: What time do you usually go to sleep?
follow_ups.response: Around 11:30, though I sometimes stay up too late reading.

follow_ups.question: What is your most fixed weekly activity?
follow_ups.response: Sunday call with Denise and Saturday pickleball, when weather and knees cooperate.

transcript.question_text: At what kind of job or jobs do you work, and when do you work?
transcript.response: I am mostly a retail operations consultant now, after decades as an operations manager. I help small businesses with inventory, budgeting, scheduling, POS reports, and Excel or Google Sheets dashboards. Some work is remote from my apartment, and some is on site in Brooklyn shops. I usually work 20 to 25 hours a week, though it changes by client. I prefer mornings because my mind is sharper before the phone starts ringing.

follow_ups.question: What kind of clients do you like best?
follow_ups.response: Family-owned stores where the owner knows the business but needs structure.

follow_ups.question: What work do you dislike?
follow_ups.response: Cleaning up chaotic records with no naming system. I can do it, but it tests my patience.

transcript.question_text: Do you have other routines or responsibilities that you did not already share?
transcript.response: I keep up with household bills, my own health appointments, and checking in on my sister. I also maintain a little balcony garden with basil, parsley, and micro-greens. A few evenings a week I do puzzles or work in the spare room on a small woodworking project. I try to walk three mornings a week with a senior walking group in spring and fall.

follow_ups.question: What do you cook most often?
follow_ups.response: Pasta with herb pesto, ramen with miso and greens, and a grilled cheese when I am tired.

follow_ups.question: What are you building now?
follow_ups.response: A narrow side table for the hallway, nothing fancy, just sturdy.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about any recent changes to your daily routine.
transcript.response: The big change is moving away from full-time management. I no longer have to be the first call when someone calls out sick or a delivery is wrong. That has lowered my stress, but it also left empty space in the day. I have been trying to fill that space with better routines, like walking, photography, and sorting old family records. Some days I do well; some days my notes are everywhere and I circle the same task three times.

follow_ups.question: Do you miss the old pace?
follow_ups.response: I miss being needed, but I do not miss constant interruptions.

follow_ups.question: What new routine has stuck best?
follow_ups.response: Morning coffee with a written task list. If I skip it, the day gets loose.

transcript.question_text: If you have children, tell me about a typical weekday during the school year for your children. What is their daily routine? And what are after school activities your children participate in?
transcript.response: I do not have children, so that does not apply to me directly. I have heard enough from my sister and niece to know school schedules can run a household, but I never had that responsibility myself.

follow_ups.question: Did you help with nieces or nephews when they were young?
follow_ups.response: Sometimes, especially pickups or watching them for a few hours, but I was not a daily caregiver.

follow_ups.question: Did not having children shape your work life?
follow_ups.response: Yes. I had more flexibility for long hours, but maybe too much of my identity went into work.

transcript.question_text: Some people we've talked to tell us about experiences with law enforcement. How about for you?
transcript.response: I have not been arrested, but I have had encounters. As a young Black man in Brooklyn, you learned early that police might stop you for no clear reason. Once in my twenties, walking home from the train, two officers questioned me like I had done something. Nothing happened, but the feeling stays with you. Later, as a manager, I dealt with police for shoplifting incidents or disputes outside the store. I learned to stay calm, speak clearly, and watch how quickly things could escalate.

follow_ups.question: What did that stop in your twenties teach you?
follow_ups.response: That being respectable does not always protect you. You still have to manage how others see you.

follow_ups.question: Did work change how you interacted with police?
follow_ups.response: Yes, I had to be practical and document everything, even when I was uneasy.

transcript.question_text: What other experiences with law enforcement stand out in your mind?
transcript.response: The stop-and-frisk years stand out. Even when it did not happen to me directly, younger staff would come in angry or embarrassed after being stopped.

follow_ups.question: How did you respond to those younger staff?
follow_ups.response: I listened first, then made sure they were okay to work or needed a minute.

follow_ups.question: Did you ever file a complaint?
follow_ups.response: No, I never did. Back then I did not think it would go anywhere.

transcript.question_text: Some people tell us about experiences of arrest -- of loved ones, family members, friends, or themselves. How about for you?
transcript.response: I was never arrested. I had a cousin who was arrested for a drug-related charge years ago, and it shook the family, but he eventually rebuilt his life.

follow_ups.question: Were you close to that cousin?
follow_ups.response: Not very close, but close enough to see what it did to his mother.

follow_ups.question: Did it change how you saw the system?
follow_ups.response: It confirmed for me that punishment and repair are not the same thing.

transcript.question_text: Some people say they vote in every election, some tell us they don't vote at all. How about you?
transcript.response: I vote regularly. I have missed a few small local primaries over the years, but I vote in presidential, mayoral, governor, and most city elections. My parents treated voting as something people paid for with sacrifice. I also know local offices matter: sanitation, schools, policing, small business rules, transit. I read candidate guides and usually know who I am voting for before I get to the poll site.

follow_ups.question: Do you vote early or on Election Day?
follow_ups.response: Usually Election Day, early in the morning.

follow_ups.question: Do you discuss your vote with family?
follow_ups.response: With Denise sometimes, but I do not argue politics at gatherings.

transcript.question_text: How would you describe your political views?
transcript.response: I would say I am a moderate Democrat with progressive instincts on some issues. I believe in civil rights, labor dignity, public education, health care access, and fair policing. I also believe programs have to work in real life, not just sound good at a rally. Coming from retail operations, I look at execution. Who is accountable? How does the money flow? Does the person at the counter actually get helped? Race matters to how I see politics because I grew up watching what disinvestment does to neighborhoods, and I also saw how strong communities could be when institutions did not show up. I am not anti-business. Small businesses kept a lot of families afloat. But I do not have much patience for corporations squeezing workers and then calling it efficiency. Politically, I trust people who can hold both justice and competence in the same hand.

follow_ups.question: What issues move your vote most?
follow_ups.response: Health care, housing costs, transit, policing, and whether small businesses can survive.

follow_ups.question: Do you belong to any political organization?
follow_ups.response: No. I vote and read, but I am not a club member or campaign volunteer.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about any recent changes in your political views.
transcript.response: I have become more concerned about housing and older people being priced out. When I was younger, I thought if you worked steadily, you could carve out a secure place. Now I see people doing everything right and still getting squeezed. I am also more skeptical of big promises from politicians. The pandemic years made me pay attention to how fragile systems are. At the same time, I have become more sympathetic to younger people asking for deeper change, even when I think their language can be sharper than mine.

follow_ups.question: What made housing feel more urgent?
follow_ups.response: Seeing longtime neighbors leave and younger workers unable to rent near their jobs.

follow_ups.question: Have younger relatives influenced you?
follow_ups.response: Yes, Tasha especially. She pushes me to see how debt and rent shape her generation.

transcript.question_text: One topic a lot of people have been talking about recently is race and/or racism and policing. Some tell us issues raised by the Black Lives Matter movement have affected them a lot, some say they've affected them somewhat, others say they haven't affected them at all. How about for you?
transcript.response: They affected me a lot, though not because the issues were new. For Black people my age, the shock was seeing things we had talked about privately become national conversation. George Floyd's murder was painful to watch, and I did not keep replaying the video. But I paid attention to the protests and the arguments afterward. It brought up old memories of being watched, questioned, and treated like a problem before you open your mouth.

follow_ups.question: Did you attend protests?
follow_ups.response: I attended one quiet local march, masked, but I mostly supported from a distance.

follow_ups.question: Why from a distance?
follow_ups.response: Crowds make me anxious, and during COVID I was careful.

transcript.question_text: How have you been thinking about the issues Black Lives Matter raises?
transcript.response: I think the core issue is dignity and accountability. People sometimes make it too abstract. I think about a young man walking home and whether he is treated like somebody's son or like a threat. I also think about budgets, training, civilian oversight, and what we ask police to handle that should be handled by mental health workers or community services. The phrase can get politicized, but the human concern underneath it is very real to me.

follow_ups.question: What reform seems most practical to you?
follow_ups.response: Real accountability records and trained non-police crisis response for mental health calls.

follow_ups.question: Do you talk about this with older friends?
follow_ups.response: Yes, but quietly. Many of us have stories, and not everyone wants to relive them.

transcript.question_text: How have you been thinking about race in the U.S. recently?
transcript.response: I think the country keeps trying to skip the hard reading assignment. People want reconciliation without memory. My own family story is migration, work, exclusion, neighborhood pride, and constant adaptation. Recently I have been reading more about redlining and urban renewal because it explains what I saw as a child. I do not walk around angry every day, but I do not confuse quiet with forgetting.

follow_ups.question: What have you read recently on this?
follow_ups.response: Books and articles on redlining, Black migration, and how highways cut through neighborhoods.

follow_ups.question: Do you share that history with younger relatives?
follow_ups.response: Yes, especially when they ask about where our grandparents came from.

transcript.question_text: How have you responded to the increased focus on race and/or racism and policing? Some people tell us they're aware of the issue but keep their thoughts to themselves, others say they've talked to family and friends, others have joined protests. What about you?
transcript.response: I have talked with family and a few friends, attended one local march, donated a small amount to a legal aid group, and gone to Black history exhibits. Mostly I respond by staying informed and mentoring younger people to protect themselves and still expect dignity.

follow_ups.question: Where did you march?
follow_ups.response: In Brooklyn, not far from Prospect Park, during the early protest period.

follow_ups.question: What do you tell younger people?
follow_ups.response: Keep records, know your rights, stay calm if you can, and do not let unfair treatment define your worth.

transcript.question_text: What about people you're close to? How have they responded to the increased focus on race and/or racism and policing?
transcript.response: My sister was deeply affected and worried about her son, even though Marcus is grown. Tasha was more activist and posted a lot online. Calvin is closer to me: concerned, thoughtful, but not interested in shouting matches. Some older relatives feel tired, like they have been explaining the same thing for fifty years.

follow_ups.question: Did it create disagreements?
follow_ups.response: A few, mostly about tactics and slogans, not about whether racism exists.

follow_ups.question: Who was most vocal?
follow_ups.response: Tasha. She is the one who pushes the family group chat.

transcript.question_text: Now we'd like to learn more about your health. First, tell me all about your health.
transcript.response: Overall, I am doing all right for 64. I have some knee aches, especially after pickleball or when I forget to stretch. My blood pressure has been borderline, so I watch salt more than I used to. I wear reading glasses, and my sleep is decent but not perfect. I am not a gym person, but I walk and try to keep moving. I could stand to lose a few pounds, mostly from sitting at the desk and snacking at night.

follow_ups.question: Do you take regular medication?
follow_ups.response: A low-dose blood pressure medication and the usual vitamins, nothing complicated.

follow_ups.question: How often do you see a doctor?
follow_ups.response: Primary care once or twice a year, more if something comes up.

transcript.question_text: For you, what makes it easy or hard to stay healthy?
transcript.response: Easy is that I can cook, walk, and live near stores with fresh produce. Hard is habit. I get wrapped up in a spreadsheet or a book and sit too long. I also forget stretching until my knee reminds me. Stress makes me snack, especially crackers and cheese late at night.

follow_ups.question: What healthy habit are you most consistent about?
follow_ups.response: Walking when the weather is decent.

follow_ups.question: What food is hardest to limit?
follow_ups.response: Sharp cheddar. A grilled cheese is my comfort meal.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about anything big that has happened in the past two years related to your health: any medical diagnoses, flare-ups of chronic conditions, broken bones, pain -- anything like that.
transcript.response: Nothing dramatic like a broken bone. The main thing was my doctor telling me to take blood pressure more seriously. I also had a knee flare after a pickleball game last summer because I played too long and skipped stretching. It swelled a little, so I rested, iced it, and did a few physical therapy exercises I found from a prior visit. That made me accept that I am not thirty anymore.

follow_ups.question: Did the knee keep you home?
follow_ups.response: For a couple days I avoided stairs and skipped walking club.

follow_ups.question: Did you change anything after the blood pressure talk?
follow_ups.response: Less salty takeout, more home cooking, and I check it at the pharmacy sometimes.

transcript.question_text: Sometimes, health problems get in the way. They can even affect people's ability to work or care for their children. How about you?
transcript.response: My health has not stopped me from working, but the knee affects how long I want to be on my feet at a client site. I plan more desk work now and avoid carrying heavy boxes.

follow_ups.question: Do clients accommodate that?
follow_ups.response: Usually, yes. I am there for analysis and systems now, not lifting cases.

follow_ups.question: Does stress affect work?
follow_ups.response: If I let worry build up, I overcheck everything and waste time.

transcript.question_text: Sometimes, it's not your health problem, but the health of a loved one. Has this been an issue for you?
transcript.response: Yes, especially when my parents were aging. My mother had diabetes complications, and my father had heart issues. Those years taught me how draining appointments, insurance calls, and medication schedules can be. Right now my sister has some arthritis, and I check on her, but she manages. I worry about being alone if my own health changes later.

follow_ups.question: Were you a caregiver for your parents?
follow_ups.response: Part-time, yes. Denise did more hands-on, but I handled paperwork and appointments.

follow_ups.question: Does that affect your planning now?
follow_ups.response: Definitely. I keep documents organized and think about who could help if I needed it.

transcript.question_text: Tell me what it has been like trying to get the health care you or your immediate family need. Have you ever had to forgo getting the health care you need?
transcript.response: I have been fortunate to have coverage through work and now a mix of coverage as I transition. I have delayed dental work before because of cost. Specialist appointments can take too long, and insurance paperwork is a headache. I would not say I have gone without major care, but I have postponed things until the bill felt manageable.

follow_ups.question: What care did you postpone?
follow_ups.response: A crown and some follow-up dental work.

follow_ups.question: Do you trust your primary doctor?
follow_ups.response: Yes. She is direct and does not rush me too much.

transcript.question_text: Have you or your immediate family ever used alternative forms of medicine? This might include indigenous, non-western, or informal forms of care.
transcript.response: Mostly home remedies, nothing formal. My mother believed in ginger tea, honey, Vicks, Epsom salt soaks, and certain foods when you were run down. I still use ginger tea and warm compresses. I believe in doctors, but I also believe a good soup and rest can do what they are supposed to do.

follow_ups.question: Do you use herbs from your balcony for that?
follow_ups.response: Sometimes mint or basil in tea or cooking, but I do not treat it like medicine.

follow_ups.question: Any supplements?
follow_ups.response: Vitamin D and a basic multivitamin.

transcript.question_text: During tough times, some people tell us they cope by smoking or drinking. How about for you?
transcript.response: I do not smoke. I drink lightly, maybe a beer with a game or a glass of bourbon on a cold evening, but not every week. During tough times I am more likely to withdraw, play jazz, clean a drawer, or make a spreadsheet nobody asked for. That is my way of getting control back.

follow_ups.question: Did you ever smoke?
follow_ups.response: I tried cigarettes when I was young, but it never became a habit.

follow_ups.question: What do you drink most often?
follow_ups.response: A single beer during a Knicks or Yankees game.

transcript.question_text: Other people say they cope by relying on prescriptions, pain medications, marijuana, or other substances. How about for you and can you describe your most recent experience of using them, if any?
transcript.response: I do not use marijuana or other substances. For pain, I use over-the-counter ibuprofen once in a while, mostly for the knee. The last time was after pickleball, when I overdid it. I took two tablets with food, iced the knee, and skipped the next walk. I am cautious with medication because I saw older relatives end up with too many pills.

follow_ups.question: Any prescription pain medication?
follow_ups.response: No.

follow_ups.question: What do you do before taking ibuprofen?
follow_ups.response: Stretch, ice, rest, and see if it settles on its own.

transcript.question_text: How are you and your family coping with, or paying for, your health care needs right now?
transcript.response: I budget for premiums, copays, and prescriptions. It is manageable, but I keep an eye on it because consulting income varies. Denise has her own coverage. We both try to stay ahead of appointments so problems do not become emergencies. Dental is the weak spot financially.

follow_ups.question: Do medical bills create stress?
follow_ups.response: Not monthly, but the surprise ones do.

follow_ups.question: Do you use savings for care?
follow_ups.response: For dental, yes, sometimes.

transcript.question_text: Some people are excited about medical vaccination, and others, not so much. How about you?
transcript.response: I am pro-vaccine. I got COVID shots and boosters, and I get the flu shot. I understand mistrust in Black communities because history gives reasons, but I look at the evidence and talk to my doctor.

follow_ups.question: Did you have side effects?
follow_ups.response: Sore arm and tired for a day.

follow_ups.question: Did family agree?
follow_ups.response: Mostly yes, though a couple cousins were hesitant.

transcript.question_text: What are your trusted sources of information about the vaccine?
transcript.response: My primary doctor first. Then the CDC site, New York City health department information, and mainstream reporting from places like NPR or the Times. I do not take medical advice from Facebook comments. If something sounds dramatic, I check more than one source.

follow_ups.question: Do you read scientific studies directly?
follow_ups.response: Sometimes the summaries, but I am not a medical scientist.

follow_ups.question: Who do you distrust?
follow_ups.response: Influencers selling certainty and supplements at the same time.

transcript.question_text: Now we're going to talk a bit more about what life was like for you over the past year. Tell me all about how you have been feeling.
transcript.response: This past year has been mixed. I feel relieved not to be carrying full-time operations stress, but I also feel unmoored sometimes. Work gave my days structure and a reason people needed me. Now I have to build that structure myself. I worry about money, health, and getting older alone. But I also have peaceful days: jazz playing, sunlight on the balcony, a good photograph coming out right. I would not call myself unhappy. I would say I am adjusting.

follow_ups.question: When do you feel best?
follow_ups.response: Morning, after coffee, when I know what the day is supposed to be.

follow_ups.question: When do you feel worst?
follow_ups.response: Late evening if I have been alone all day and did not finish what I planned.

transcript.question_text: Tell me a story about a time in the last year when you were in a rough place or struggling emotionally.
transcript.response: Last winter I had a week where two consulting invoices were late, my knee hurt, and the apartment felt too quiet. I sat at the kitchen table surrounded by receipts and old notes, and I could not make myself start. That is unusual for me. I finally called Denise, not to ask for money, just to hear a familiar voice. Then I put on Coltrane, cleared one stack at a time, and made a simple dinner. It did not solve everything, but it got me moving.

follow_ups.question: Was it hard to call your sister?
follow_ups.response: A little. I do not like sounding needy.

follow_ups.question: What song or album did you play?
follow_ups.response: Coltrane's Ballads album. It steadies me.

transcript.question_text: Some people say they struggle with depression, anxiety, or something else like that. How about for you?
transcript.response: I would say I have anxiety, mostly worry and overthinking. I have never been formally diagnosed with major depression, and I do not want to claim what is not mine, but I do have low spells. Anxiety shows up as making too many lists, checking numbers repeatedly, or avoiding a phone call because I imagine it going badly. I manage it with routine, walking, music, and talking to a few trusted people.

follow_ups.question: Have you seen a therapist?
follow_ups.response: Briefly after my mother died. It helped, but I did not continue long term.

follow_ups.question: Would you consider therapy again?
follow_ups.response: Yes, if worry started interfering more.

transcript.question_text: How has it been for your family?
transcript.response: My family is mostly managing, but everyone has their pressures. Denise worries about health and her kids. The younger ones worry about rent, debt, and job stability. We are not a family that talks about feelings easily, but we check in.

follow_ups.question: Who talks most openly?
follow_ups.response: Tasha. She names things the older generation would talk around.

follow_ups.question: How do you show concern?
follow_ups.response: I call, ask practical questions, and offer help with forms or budgeting.

transcript.question_text: Some people say that religion or spirituality is important in their lives, for others not so much. How about you?
transcript.response: I was raised in the Black Baptist church tradition, though I am not a regular churchgoer now. My mother believed in church as worship and community. I still respect that deeply. These days I would call myself culturally Christian and quietly spiritual. I may go on Easter, for a funeral, or if my sister asks me to attend something. I pray sometimes, usually short prayers of gratitude or worry. I also find something spiritual in music, woodworking, and walking through old Brooklyn streets thinking about the people who came before me.

follow_ups.question: Do you belong to a congregation now?
follow_ups.response: No, not formally.

follow_ups.question: What part of church stayed with you?
follow_ups.response: The music, the call-and-response, and the idea that people look after one another.

transcript.question_text: Some people tell us they use Facebook, Instagram, or other social media to stay connected with the wider world. How about for you? Tell me all about how you use these types of platforms.
transcript.response: I use Facebook lightly, mostly for family updates, old neighborhood groups, and local history pages. I have Instagram but mostly look at photography accounts, jazz record collectors, and museum pages. I do not post daily. Maybe I put up a black-and-white street photo once every few weeks. I avoid arguments. Social media can be useful, but it also makes people perform certainty.

follow_ups.question: What local pages do you follow?
follow_ups.response: Brooklyn history groups, Black history organizations, and a few neighborhood event pages.

follow_ups.question: Do you use Twitter or X?
follow_ups.response: No, I stopped looking at it. Too much noise.

transcript.question_text: Some people say they use Facebook or Twitter to get (emotional or financial) support during tough times. What about you?
transcript.response: No, I do not use social media for support like that. If I am in trouble, I call my sister or a close friend. I am private about hardship.

follow_ups.question: Have you donated to others online?
follow_ups.response: A few times, for medical fundraisers when I knew the family.

follow_ups.question: Why not ask online yourself?
follow_ups.response: Pride, privacy, and not wanting my business public.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about any recent changes in your level of stress, worry, and your emotional coping strategies.
transcript.response: My work stress is lower, but life-planning worry is higher. I cope more intentionally now: walks, written budgets, jazz, fewer late-night news spirals, and trying to call people before I get too isolated.

follow_ups.question: What news habit did you change?
follow_ups.response: I stopped checking headlines right before bed.

follow_ups.question: What works best?
follow_ups.response: Walking and writing down the actual numbers instead of imagining them.

transcript.question_text: Bills can fluctuate over the course of a year. Seasons change, there are holidays and special events, school starts and ends, and so on. Tell me all about how your bills have fluctuated over the past year.
transcript.response: Utilities rise in summer with the air conditioner and in winter with heat-related costs. Holidays bring gifts and travel to family. Health and dental are the unpredictable ones. Food costs have also crept up, even when I cook at home.

follow_ups.question: Which month is hardest?
follow_ups.response: December, because gifts, food, and year-end bills all stack up.

follow_ups.question: Do consulting slowdowns affect bills?
follow_ups.response: Yes, especially in late summer when clients delay projects.

transcript.question_text: Tell me all about how you coped with any extra expenses in the past months.
transcript.response: I used savings for the dental bill, delayed buying a new camera lens, and cooked more at home. I also followed up firmly on late invoices.

follow_ups.question: Do you use credit cards for gaps?
follow_ups.response: Sometimes for timing, but I try to pay them off monthly.

follow_ups.question: What did you cook more of?
follow_ups.response: Soup, pasta, ramen with greens, and rice dishes.

transcript.question_text: Some people have a savings account, some people save in a different way, and some people say they don't save. How about you?
transcript.response: I save, though not as much as I wish I had when I was younger. I have a savings account, retirement accounts from work, and a small brokerage account. I am cautious. I like to know I can cover rent and medical costs if work slows down. Consulting income is less predictable, so I keep a buffer.

follow_ups.question: How many months of expenses do you aim for?
follow_ups.response: At least six months, though I am not always at that mark.

follow_ups.question: Who taught you to save?
follow_ups.response: My parents taught thrift, but not investing. Investing I learned late.

transcript.question_text: Some people save for big things, like a home, while others save for a rainy day. How about for you (in the last year)?
transcript.response: Mostly rainy day and retirement. I also have a small travel fund for a trip to Kyoto someday, though I keep postponing it because I over-research and worry about logistics. I save for practical peace: health costs, rent increases, replacing a laptop, things like that.

follow_ups.question: Why Kyoto?
follow_ups.response: Gardens, craft, old streets, quiet temples, and photography.

follow_ups.question: What keeps delaying it?
follow_ups.response: Flight planning, cost, language worries, and my habit of trying to perfect the itinerary.

transcript.question_text: Some people have student loans or credit card debt. Others take out loans from family or friends or find other ways of borrowing money. Tell me about all the debts you're paying on right now.
transcript.response: No student loans now. I have regular credit card balances during the month, but I try not to carry them. No family loans. The main obligation is rent and ordinary monthly bills.

follow_ups.question: Did you ever have education debt?
follow_ups.response: A little, but I paid it off years ago.

follow_ups.question: Any car loan?
follow_ups.response: No car.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about any time during the past year that you haven't had enough money to buy something that you needed or pay a bill that was due.
transcript.response: I did not miss a bill, but there were tight moments. When invoices came late and the dental bill hit, I delayed nonurgent purchases and moved money from savings. I needed new shoes but waited a month. That is not crisis poverty, but it reminds you how quickly things can tighten when income is variable.

follow_ups.question: Did you ask anyone for help?
follow_ups.response: No.

follow_ups.question: What bill worries you most?
follow_ups.response: Rent, because everything else organizes around that.

transcript.question_text: What is or was your occupation? In this occupation, what kind of work do you do and what are the most important activities or duties?
transcript.response: My occupation was retail operations manager, and now I am transitioning into operations consulting. As a manager I handled inventory control, purchasing, staff scheduling, budgets, vendor issues, customer problems, POS reports, and sometimes basic IT troubleshooting. The most important duty was keeping the business running without drama. That means enough staff on the floor, enough product in stock, not too much cash tied up in slow inventory, and clear procedures when something goes wrong. I became good at building Excel and Google Sheets dashboards to show sales trends, stock levels, labor hours, and shrinkage. These days I advise small businesses on those same systems.

follow_ups.question: What task are you best at?
follow_ups.response: Finding where money or time is leaking in a process.

follow_ups.question: What kind of mentoring do you do?
follow_ups.response: One-on-one coaching for younger managers on scheduling, conflict, and reading reports.

transcript.question_text: Was your occupation covered by a union or employee association contract?
transcript.response: No, my management role was not union-covered. Some workers in similar sectors had associations, but my position was salaried management.

follow_ups.question: Did you support union workers generally?
follow_ups.response: Yes, I understand why workers need protection.

follow_ups.question: Did lack of union affect you?
follow_ups.response: It meant I had to negotiate for myself.

transcript.response: About 48 weeks. Some weeks were only a few consulting hours, but I worked through most of the year.

follow_ups.response: Not formal sick leave, just rescheduling client work.

transcript.response: Usually around 25 hours now.

follow_ups.response: Yes, 45 to 50 hours in full-time management.

follow_ups.response: Not much more, maybe steadier hours.

follow_ups.response: Both: one client visit and several remote hours.

follow_ups.response: Occasionally, but I try to avoid it.

follow_ups.question: Any side selling or gig work?
follow_ups.response: No.

transcript.response: One self-employed consulting line of work, with three paying clients that month.

follow_ups.response: Two retail, one small service business.

follow_ups.response: Yes, one younger manager I advise informally.

follow_ups.response: Yes, I move a percentage into a separate account.

transcript.response: Irregularly, usually when invoices are paid, often every two weeks but not guaranteed.

follow_ups.question: How do you manage that?
follow_ups.response: I keep a buffer and send reminders.

transcript.response: Since I live alone, household income is my income. Last month it was about $4,800 before taxes.

follow_ups.response: Not yet. I am planning when to claim.

follow_ups.question: Did you owe or receive a refund?
follow_ups.response: I owed a modest amount.

follow_ups.question: Do you keep receipts organized?
follow_ups.response: Eventually. During the year they get messy.

transcript.question_text: Tell me more about your workplace. How long have you been at your current job? How would you describe the benefits that come with your job? (This could include things like health benefits, paid time off, vacation, and sick time.)
transcript.response: I have been consulting about two years. As self-employed, benefits are my responsibility, so there is flexibility but no paid vacation or sick time.

follow_ups.question: Do you miss employer benefits?
follow_ups.response: Yes, especially health coverage simplicity.

follow_ups.question: What is the upside?
follow_ups.response: Control over my schedule.

transcript.question_text: How would you describe your relationships at work? (How is your relationship with your manager or boss? How are your relationships with your coworkers?)
transcript.response: I do not have a boss now. Client relationships are respectful, and I still keep in touch with former coworkers.

follow_ups.question: Any difficult clients?
follow_ups.response: A few who resist changing habits.

follow_ups.question: Do former staff call you?
follow_ups.response: Yes, sometimes for advice.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about how predictable your work schedule is. How would you describe your job in terms of flexibility with your hours?
transcript.response: The schedule is flexible but not always predictable. I can decide many of my hours, which I like, but clients call when they have problems. I try to reserve mornings for focused dashboard or budget work and afternoons for calls. Compared with management, it is much more flexible. Compared with a steady paycheck job, it can feel uncertain.

follow_ups.question: Do you work evenings?
follow_ups.response: Only if a deadline is close.

follow_ups.question: What makes a week unpredictable?
follow_ups.response: Inventory errors, payroll deadlines, or a client suddenly needing a report.

transcript.question_text: Some people say it's hard to take or keep a job because of child care. How about for you?
transcript.response: Child care is not an issue for me because I do not have children.

follow_ups.response: Many times, yes.

follow_ups.question: Did that shape scheduling?
follow_ups.response: Definitely. Good scheduling has to respect real lives.

follow_ups.response: No.

follow_ups.response: No.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about times over the last year when your income was especially low. And tell me about all the things you did to make ends meet during that time.
transcript.response: Late summer was slow. I reduced discretionary spending, followed up on outstanding invoices, used a little savings, cooked at home, and delayed buying photo paper and tools. I also reached out to two former contacts and picked up a short dashboard cleanup project.

follow_ups.question: What did you cut first?

follow_ups.question: Did you feel panicked?
follow_ups.response: Not panicked, but tense.

transcript.response: I could cover $400 from savings. I would not enjoy it, but it would not break me. If it came during a tight month, I might put it on a credit card and pay it off when invoices came in.

follow_ups.question: What emergency do you worry about most?
follow_ups.response: Dental, medical, or a laptop failure.

follow_ups.question: Would you ask family?

transcript.question_text: Overall, how do you feel about your financial situation?
transcript.response: Cautiously okay. I am not wealthy, and I wish I had started investing earlier, but I have skills, some savings, and low extravagant tastes. My biggest concern is aging in New York with rent and health costs. I want enough passive income and consulting work to live modestly without constant pressure. I do not need luxury. I need stability, quiet, and the ability to say no to work that is not worth the stress.

follow_ups.question: What would make you feel secure?

follow_ups.question: Do you budget monthly?

follow_ups.response: Yes, and the hours could be tiring.

follow_ups.question: Did her work influence you?
follow_ups.response: It taught me patience and respect for service work.

transcript.question_text: What kind of place did she work for? What kind of business was it? What did they make or do where she worked?
transcript.response: She worked in a nursing home and later a hospital setting in Brooklyn. They provided patient care, especially for older people and people recovering from illness. It was hard work and not paid enough for what it required.

follow_ups.question: Did you ever visit her workplace?
follow_ups.response: A few times, mostly waiting in the lobby.

follow_ups.question: How did she talk about work?
follow_ups.response: Tired, but proud when she could help someone.

transcript.question_text: Did your dad work for pay for at least a year while you were growing up?
transcript.response: Yes.

follow_ups.question: Was he steady in work?
follow_ups.response: Very steady.

follow_ups.question: Did he retire from that field?
follow_ups.response: He stayed in similar work until later life.

transcript.question_text: What was his job? What kind of work did he do? What were his most important activities or duties?
transcript.response: My father worked in building maintenance, mostly for apartment buildings. He handled repairs, boilers, cleaning common areas, small plumbing issues, and making sure tenants had heat and basics. He was good with his hands and believed a man should know how to fix things.

follow_ups.question: Did he teach you tools?
follow_ups.response: Yes, that is where my woodworking comfort started.

follow_ups.question: What was his strongest lesson?
follow_ups.response: Do the job right even if nobody is watching.

transcript.question_text: What kind of place did he work for? What kind of business was it? What did they make or do where he worked?
transcript.response: He worked for property management companies that maintained residential apartment buildings. They provided housing, collected rent, and handled repairs. He was part of the crew that kept buildings livable.

follow_ups.question: Was it union work?
follow_ups.response: Some jobs had union connections, but I do not remember every detail.

follow_ups.question: Did tenants know him?
follow_ups.response: Yes, many knew him by name.

transcript.question_text: We all have hopes about what our future will look like. Imagine yourself a few years from now. Maybe you want your life to be the same in some ways as it is now. Maybe you want it to be different in some ways. What do you hope for?
transcript.response: A few years from now, I hope to be semi-retired in a real way, not just between obligations. I would like a small, steady consulting practice with clients I respect, maybe two or three businesses at a time. I want to run a short mentorship program for younger managers in Brooklyn, especially people who know the work but never got formal guidance. I hope my health stays good enough for walking, travel, and pickleball if I remember to stretch. I would like to finally take the Kyoto trip and stop trying to make the perfect itinerary. Mostly I want a modest, low-stress life: good coffee, jazz in the evening, family calls, meaningful work, and enough savings not to be afraid of every envelope in the mail.

follow_ups.question: What would the mentorship program teach first?
follow_ups.response: Scheduling fairly, reading basic financial reports, and handling conflict without losing people.

follow_ups.question: What would a good ordinary day look like?
follow_ups.response: Morning walk, two focused work hours, lunch at home, photography in the afternoon, music at night.

transcript.question_text: What do you value the most in your life?
transcript.response: I value steadiness, dignity, usefulness, and memory. By memory I mean family history, neighborhood history, knowing how people survived and built something. I value quiet, but not emptiness. I value being someone people can trust with a problem. I also value craft, whether that is a clean spreadsheet, a well-made table, a good photograph, or a pot of greens cooked the way my mother would recognize.

follow_ups.question: What value did your parents give you most strongly?
follow_ups.response: Do not waste what you have, and do not look down on working people.

follow_ups.question: What do you want people to say about you?
follow_ups.response: That I was reliable, fair, and paid attention.
